title: {{NAME}} and the World Cup of the Wildwood
moral: When everyone plays to their own strengths, every team can win.
character_anchor: Bright children's book cartoon illustration, bold outlines, vivid flat colours. {{NAME}}, a young boy with brown hair and blue eyes, wearing a bright orange soccer jersey, navy shorts, and orange-and-white cleats — same child, same face, same exact outfit in every image.

pages.content:
{{NAME}} had lost every football match that season.

Not because he was bad. But his team had six players and the other teams always had twelve and had practised more.

So when the animals of Pinewood Park challenged him to a match on Saturday morning, a sign scratched into the mud at the park gate, {{NAME}} said yes before he could think about it.

Then he thought about it. The animals had drawn a football boot and a small badger wearing a headband.

"Fair enough," he said.

pages.content:
The animal team arrived at nine sharp.

Goalkeeper: a very round badger who could spread his considerable body across the full lower half of the goal.

Midfielders: three rabbits who moved so fast they left afterimages.

Striker: a fox who moved with such elegant precision it was almost unfair.

Defence: two deer who were, collectively, about six feet tall.

{{NAME}} looked at them. He looked at his team.

"Different problem, different solution," he said. "Listen up."

pages.content:
{{NAME}}'s plan: use the animals' own approach against them.

He put Soren head-to-head with the fox, because Soren was best at mirroring an opponent's movement.

He told his defenders to aim every clearance at the rabbits, not away from them, because rabbits flinch at incoming balls.

For the badger goalkeeper: aim high every single time, because the badger's reach was horizontal perfection but his vertical was limited.

At half time: {{NAME}}'s team two, Animals two.

pages.content:
With two minutes left, {{NAME}} had the ball at the edge of the box.

The badger spread his arms. The deer loomed. The rabbits flanked.

{{NAME}} paused. Everyone froze.

Then he looked up, not at the goal, but at his teammate Maya cutting in from the left, completely unmarked, because every animal had watched him and forgotten to watch anyone else.

He passed. Maya shot. High corner.

The badger dove right. The ball went left. Three to two.

pages.content:
After the final whistle, the fox trotted over and touched {{NAME}}'s hand with its nose, which he understood was a compliment of the highest order.

The badger gave him a dignified nod. The rabbits ran figure eights around his ankles.

They left {{NAME}} at the park gate as the sun went down, the forest swallowing them one by one.

{{NAME}} walked home with muddy boots and a full heart, replaying Maya's goal in his head.

In the dark of his room, almost asleep, he heard it: the faint, far-off sound of a crowd of animals cheering.
